Independent construction safety analytics · Canada

Site Safety Early Warning

Which zone of a construction site is most likely to hurt someone in the next five work days, the warning signs behind it, and the controls to put in place before the shift. Built for all 10 provinces and 3 territories: calibrated to AWCBC, Statistics Canada and provincial board data, run on real Environment Canada weather, tested on 165,000 real Ontario inspections, and re-scored as forecasts change and a site logs each day.

Independent analysis by a private analyst. Not produced by, affiliated with or endorsed by any workers' compensation board, regulator or employer.

Analysis and design by Osman Zakaria, PMP

    Score your own site logs

    Upload a CSV of your site's daily zone logs and the trained model scores every zone-day: the risk of an injury or high-potential near miss in the next 5 work days, the warning signs behind it and the controls, cited for your province. Add an incidents column and it checks how many of your own incidents it would have flagged in advance. Your file is read in this browser only: it is never uploaded, saved or shared.

    1 · Get the template

    One row per zone per work day. Map each of your work areas to the nearest of the ten zone types. Weather columns are optional (the seasonal outlook fills gaps); so is the incidents column.

    Zones ranked by risk

    Check before relying on it: the model was trained on simulated logs calibrated to provincial claims data. Scoring your own history with your own incidents, as here, is how a pilot tests whether it holds for your sites.

    Monthly proof report: would it have warned you?

    Month by month on your own logs: incidents, how many had an amber or red warning in the 5 work days before, and the incident rate on red days. Controls your supervisors recorded as done are measured by how much each one lowered its zone's modelled risk.

    Look-ahead: catch clashes before they're scheduled

    Load your 2- or 3-week look-ahead. Each activity is checked against the weather, the other trades in its zone and any crane lifts overhead. Each zone-day is also scored with the trained model. Every clash comes with a fix you can apply here, which re-checks the plan straight away.

    Report a near miss or hazard

    For the site: put this on the gate

    Workers scan the code to report in their own language. Reports are anonymous: no name or account is stored with them. In this prototype the page has to be shared with the person reporting; a product version would take reports by text message.

    Reports received

    Form wording in French, Spanish, Portuguese, Tagalog, Punjabi and Chinese should be checked by a native speaker before site use.

    Photo check: hazards from site photos

    To check every working zone in turn, use the photo walk in the Daily log tab. Here you can check a single batch: add photos from a site walk. Claude looks at each one for fall, PPE, housekeeping, excavation, scaffold, lifting, traffic and electrical hazards, marks roughly where each one is, and the page turns the findings into the zone's readings: hazard observations, PPE gaps and housekeeping. The trained model then re-scores the zone's 5-day risk, and every finding comes with the control and legal citation from the control library.

    1 · Photos and where they were taken

    Add up to a few photos at a time.

    Before you upload

    • Where the photos go: to Claude, on your own Claude account, for this analysis only. The page doesn't store them, and the downloaded report keeps them only if you save it.
    • People in photos: Claude is told to judge equipment and conditions, never to identify anyone. Avoid close-up faces and name badges where you can.
    • It's a second pair of eyes. Locations are approximate and a photo shows one moment. A competent person confirms each finding before acting; that confirmation is what goes into the log.
    • Best results: wide shots of the work area in good light, one zone per batch.

    Forecast: the weeks ahead

    Pick a start date and a scenario. Every work day is simulated on the project calendar (crews by zone for that stage of the build) under each of the three recorded years of real Vancouver weather for those dates, scored by the trained model, and averaged. The result is each zone's risk day by day and the number of injuries and high-potential near misses to expect.

    Reading it honestly

      Does it work?

      Judged only on the ten months after training, across 30 sites in three provinces. The comparison that matters is against knowing how many people will be in each zone, which a schedule already tells a superintendent.

      Event rate by alert band (test period)

      Which signals carry the warning (AUC lost when each is shuffled)

      Ranking quality against two yardsticks

      The ceiling is a model that knows each zone's true hidden hazard, which no real system can see.

      Calibration: predicted vs observed, by decile

      Real-world check: New York City construction sites

      Contractors' daily logs aren't public, so the same idea is tested on real sites and real outcomes from New York City's open records. Unit: one active construction site in one week. Question: do the warning signs a regulator already records at a site flag the sites that have a construction accident or incident in the next 4 weeks, better than the size and type of the job alone?

      On large jobs: incident rate in the next 4 weeks, with vs without each warning sign

      Large jobs = site-weeks that job size and type alone already flag. Each bar compares sites with and without one sign, so part of the gap reflects other differences between sites.

      Ranking quality (AUC, test period)

      Test-period incidents flagged in the 4 weeks before, by type

      What this shows, and what it doesn't

      Thirteen jurisdictions, one method

      Each site runs on the real weather at its nearest hourly station and is calibrated to its jurisdiction's construction lost-time claims rate. Boards differ in coverage and in what counts as lost time, so rates compare a place with itself, not with the others. Controls cite each jurisdiction's own legislation.

      Results by jurisdiction (test period, simulated logs)

      Construction lost-time claims per 100 workers, median of 2022–2024

      Construction fatalities accepted, 2022–2024 total (AWCBC; + means small counts were suppressed in some years)

      Alert cut-offs set for each jurisdiction

      One shared cut-off would under-flag low-rate places and over-alert high-rate ones. Each jurisdiction alerts at its own top 5% (red) and next 15% (amber) of zone-days in the last six months before the test, plus the wind and cold rules. Test-period alert shares run higher because the later, busier phases carry more risk.

      Read the law

      Nunavut's published consolidation doesn't yet include its 2025 amendments, and Yukon's part pages are the board's unofficial copies, so check the official version too.

      References point the site's competent person to the governing provision. Each citation links to the official text. BC, Ontario, Alberta and Yukon name parts or regulations more exactly; the others link to the whole instrument, where you search for the topic. I checked that topics appear in most of these texts by keyword, and no lawyer has reviewed them. Always check the current text.
